title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Democratic candidates differ on shielding ratepayers from AI-driven electricity costs.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're digging into the Democratic Senate primary race and a clear split on how to handle data centers pushing up everyone's electric bills.
That sounds like the heart of it. Graham, what exactly came out today from the candidates?
Michigan Public reported that the contenders laid out different plans for regulating data-center electricity demand and protecting ratepayers from new transmission costs.
So some want the utilities or the tech companies themselves to cover those upgrades, and others are okay spreading the costs across all customers?
Exactly. The exchange shows which candidates would push utilities or tech firms to cover upgrades versus spreading costs across all customers.
Why does this matter so much right now? We've been seeing these projects pop up everywhere.
Data centers need enormous amounts of power, and when demand spikes, utilities often build new lines or substations. Those costs can end up on monthly bills if they're not assigned to the big users.
And with AI driving a lot of this growth, it feels like the stakes are rising fast.
Right. Primary voters now have concrete differences on an issue that will hit monthly bills directly.
How long has this fight been building? It seems like every week another township is pausing projects.

It's been simmering for months as proposals for hyperscale campuses started hitting rural and suburban areas. Towns are worried about everything from noise and water use to farmland loss and strained grids.
And the utilities are in the middle, right? Some are trying to reassure customers.
Yes, yesterday Indiana Michigan Power pledged to shield ratepayers from data center costs in their southwest Michigan territory.
That's interesting. Do you think that pledge will hold up when the rate cases come?
Local officials and consumer groups are watching closely. These commitments sound good but often get tested in regulatory hearings.
Meanwhile DTE's earnings preview on Friday highlighted data-center growth as a profit driver. That expansion means more demand on the grid.
And that often translates into higher rates or new infrastructure costs passed to households. Michigan ratepayers have already seen added charges tied to similar projects.
So the Senate candidates are really drawing a line on whether ratepayers get protected or not.
Precisely. One approach is to make the data center operators or utilities absorb the transmission upgrades. The other is to let those costs flow into the general rate base.
What happens next in the primary? Do voters get to weigh in soon?
The differences are now on the table, so expect more debate in the coming weeks as candidates campaign on pocketbook issues like electric bills.
And on the local level, we're seeing places hit the brakes. Garfield Township froze new data centers after a sloppy filing.
Supervisors moved to block projects for at least a year. Residents near the site face uncertainty over power lines, water use, and property values.
That pause gives them time to write actual rules before anything gets locked in.
Calhoun County is weighing a similar year-long halt over jobs and power concerns. Commissioners heard worries about electricity strain and whether promised gains reach local taxpayers.
A pause there would delay projects drawing hundreds of megawatts and millions of gallons of water.
Delta County already voted Thursday to ban new data centers for a year after residents raised noise, water, and rural grid issues.
That one-year window lets officials draft permanent zoning before any large campus moves forward.
Augusta Township is nearing a vote on zoning and tax terms for a large proposal pulling power from the same DTE territory as Saline.
The outcome will decide how much new load hits ratepayers and whether the township gets meaningful revenue.
Saline Township flipped Thursday and restored Oracle's shot at a big tax break after earlier limits.
Residents now face the prospect of forgoing years of property-tax revenue on a multibillion-dollar project that would draw heavy power and water.
The change came after lobbying from the company and supporters arguing it would bring jobs.
Over in Cass County, Dowagiac residents are still dealing with noise from an operating data center's cooling systems.
The persistent humming disrupts sleep, and folks are exploring legal options including possible class-action steps.
That's a real quality-of-life issue once these places are up and running.
MLive launched a new map Thursday showing every active data center fight across the state.
It lets residents track proposals, hearings, and moratoria by township and county, with details on megawatts and tax deals.
You can see how projects near you compare to battles elsewhere.
So the big picture is towns trying to get ahead of the curve while the Senate race highlights the statewide bill impact.
Right. The primary differences on cost allocation will shape how Michigan handles this growth for years.
What do you think listeners should watch for in the next few weeks?
More rate-case filings, township votes on moratoria, and how the Senate candidates refine their positions as the primary heats up.
And of course the tracker map will keep showing where the next flashpoints are.
On deck this weekend, things are quiet with no major public hearings listed in the tracker. Keep an eye on the map for any last-minute additions.
Sounds like a good time to catch up on the existing fights.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Senate Hopefuls Split on Who Pays for Data Center Power as Local Pauses Spread
